reasons: Each stage saves its outcome and failures are recorded, which is good error handling.
No tests are visible in the provided code.
Stages after the first ones were only partly visible, so their behavior could not be fully checked.
The header says the scan is read-only, but the final step writes a run record to the Yard; what it writes is not shown here.
The truncation flag in the fetch stage is hardcoded to false.

terms.meaning: the project database the app keeps for each project
one step of a scan that saves its result before the next step begins
a named lock in the database that stops two workers from running the same run at once
a set of reusable database connections, so the app does not open a new one for every request
continue a stopped run from its first unfinished stage
the saved output of a stage, stored as structured data, which later stages read
the exact words quoted from a source
where a value came from, such as stored, calculated or directly reported
a value calculated from other values, such as percent over budget
start some work and do not wait for it to finish before replying
a written definition of the shape that data must have
text or numbers converted to a standard form so they can be compared

sections.name: File setup (part 1)
sections.title: Imported tools and modules
sections.what: Pulls in the database, the Yard record tables, web fetch and search helpers, evidence checks, calculation helpers, and the enrichment rules.
sections.why: Likely reason: the stage functions need all of these, so they are gathered in one place.
sections.watch_out: Several imports come from outside this folder, so moving files will break this runner.

sections.name: File setup (part 2)
sections.title: Design notes on the stages
sections.what: Comments that describe the seven stages, the rule that each stage reads the output of the one before it, and the promise that the scan does not write project fields.
sections.why: Explains the design to later readers.
sections.watch_out: The note says the scan is read-only, but the final step records the run in the Yard, so the note and the code do not fully agree.

sections.name: STAGE_KEYS
sections.title: Ordered list of stages
sections.what: Lists the seven stage names in running order: resolve mode, fetch, reverify, calculate, finalize, synthesis and deck model.
sections.why: Running walks this list in order, so one list keeps the order in one place.
sections.watch_out: Changing the order or the names affects resuming, because saved stages are found by these names.

sections.name: StageKey
sections.title: Type for a stage name
sections.what: Gives the code a checked type for a stage name, so a misspelled name is caught when the code is built.
sections.why: Prevents typing mistakes when stages are handled.
sections.watch_out: Older stage names saved in the database are not in this type, which is why another part of the file handles them.

sections.name: lockPool, lockPool error handler
sections.title: Dedicated database connection for locks
sections.what: Creates a small separate pool of up to four database connections used only for run locks. Locking and unlocking use the same connection, and idle connection errors are logged.
sections.why: The comment explains that a lock taken on one pooled connection cannot be released on another, and that the database frees the lock if the process dies.
sections.watch_out: The pool reads the database address from the environment when the file loads, so a missing setting makes every lock call fail.

sections.name: lockKey
sections.title: Name of a run's lock
sections.what: Builds a lock name from the run identifier, so each run has its own lock.
sections.why: One lock per run stops the same run from executing twice.
sections.watch_out: The database hashes lock names, so two different names could in theory collide, though the risk is low.

sections.name: logLine
sections.title: Timestamped log line
sections.what: Adds the current time to a message, producing a line for the stage log.
sections.why: Logs need times to help debug slow or stuck stages.
sections.watch_out: The time comes from the server clock, not the user's clock.

sections.name: getRun
sections.title: Load a run
sections.what: Reads one scan run from the database by its identifier, or returns nothing.
sections.why: Many steps check the run's current status, such as whether it was cancelled.
sections.watch_out: Each call goes to the database, so cancellation checks depend on reading fresh data.

sections.name: getStageRow
sections.title: Load one stage record
sections.what: Reads the saved record for one stage of one run.
sections.why: Used to see whether a stage already succeeded, so it is not run again.
sections.watch_out: Returns nothing if the stage has never started.

sections.name: requireStageSummary
sections.title: Read an earlier stage's output
sections.what: Returns the saved output of an earlier stage, and throws an error if that stage did not succeed or has no output.
sections.why: The comment says a later stage cannot run without the earlier one, so a missing output means the stage order was broken.
sections.watch_out: The error is thrown rather than handled here, so the calling stage is marked failed and the run stops.

sections.name: KickResult
sections.title: Possible outcomes when starting a run
sections.what: Defines what starting a run can return: success with a flag saying whether it resumed, or one of five failure codes such as not found, already running, cancelled or incompatible version.
sections.why: Lets the web routes turn each failure into the right response.
sections.watch_out: The web routes map failure codes to responses, so a new code will be returned as a conflict error.

sections.name: kickRun (part 1)
sections.title: Checks and lock before starting
sections.what: Checks that the run exists and is not cancelled or finished, refuses runs from an older version, takes the run's lock on a dedicated connection, and marks the run as running. The run counts as resumed when it was not queued.
sections.why: The lock stops two starts from running at once, and the version check stops a resume that would not be safe.
sections.watch_out: The version check relies on a marker in saved stage summaries, so a stage without that marker makes the whole run incompatible.

sections.name: kickRun (part 2)
sections.title: Launch in background and release lock
sections.what: Starts the stages without waiting for them to finish, logs any crash, and releases the lock and connection when the work ends, however it ends. The start call returns success straight away.
sections.why: Keeps the web request quick while the scan runs in the background, as the comment states.
sections.watch_out: If the process stops mid-run, nothing reports back to the user, and the run stays marked as running until someone starts it again.

sections.name: executeStages (part 1)
sections.title: Loop through stages and skip finished ones
sections.what: For each stage in order, stops if the run was cancelled, skips stages that already succeeded, records the current stage, and saves a new running record with a contract note and a fresh log.
sections.why: Skipping finished stages makes resuming safe, and the saved record keeps progress visible.
sections.watch_out: The attempt number is read from the saved contract, so damaged contract data resets the attempt count.

sections.name: executeStages (part 2)
sections.title: Run one stage and save its result
sections.what: Runs the stage while counting model usage, then saves success with output, usage and timing. On failure it saves the error message, marks the whole run failed, and stops. If the run was cancelled, it stops without saving a failure.
sections.why: Each stage's result is saved right away so a restart knows where to resume.
sections.watch_out: After a failure the run is marked failed and no later stages run until the run is started again.

sections.name: executeStages (part 3)
sections.title: Record in Yard and finish the run
sections.what: Writes the complete run to the Yard, then marks the run succeeded only if it is still running. If the Yard write fails, the run is marked failed with that reason.
sections.why: The comment says success is declared only after the Yard record is saved, so a later start can retry it.
sections.watch_out: A retry repeats the Yard write, so that write must be safe to repeat; the file relies on this without showing how it is ensured.

sections.name: FEED_FIELDS
sections.title: Labels for scan-input cards
sections.what: Maps internal field names such as planned budget, final cost and capacity to plain labels for the live feed.
sections.why: Keeps display names in one place.
sections.watch_out: Two field names share the label Capacity, and a separate rule removes the duplicate card.

sections.name: feedLabel, feedUnit, feedSkip
sections.title: Feed display rules
sections.what: Gives nuclear projects different wording for the grid connection dates, sets units such as US dollars in millions, megawatts and months, and hides a duplicate capacity card when two capacity fields hold the same number.
sections.why: The wording differs by industry, and power projects can store the same capacity twice.
sections.watch_out: The nuclear wording depends on the industry name being exactly nuclear, so renaming the industry removes it.

sections.name: DISCLOSURE_LABELS
sections.title: Labels for Yard disclosures
sections.what: Maps Yard disclosure field names, such as original budget, final cost and latest forecast completion, to readable labels with the words Yard disclosure added.
sections.why: Separates cited disclosures from stored columns in the feed.
sections.watch_out: A new disclosure key without a label has no readable name in the feed.

sections.name: SEMANTIC_TEST, hostOf
sections.title: Expected meaning per field and short site names
sections.what: The first map gives the plain statement each field must meet to count, such as a planned completion date being stated. The helper turns a web address into a short site name, or the words the source if the address is bad.
sections.why: Lets the feed explain what proof is needed and which site it came from.
sections.watch_out: The site name only drops a leading www, so other subdomains stay in the name.

sections.name: feedBasisTags
sections.title: Notes on how a budget quote was read
sections.what: Builds short tags from a quote: whether currency was converted, the price basis, whether it says estimate, and whether it states exclusions.
sections.why: Helps the reader judge a figure without reading the whole quote.
sections.watch_out: The tags come from simple word matching, so a quote saying not an estimate still gets an estimate tag.

sections.name: feedValue, fmtM, ORIGIN_WORDS
sections.title: Display formatting for values and sources
sections.what: Formats a value with its unit, showing the currency conversion for budgets when present. Also formats numbers with commas and two decimal places, and turns internal source names into plain words such as Yard field or run research.
sections.why: Makes values and sources readable in the live feed.

sections.name: emitMetricEvents
sections.title: Log lines for cost and schedule figures
sections.what: For each project, writes an event for cost deviation and for schedule overrun. A missing figure gets its reason. A present figure gets a plain formula showing its inputs and where they came from, or a note that the source reported it directly.
sections.why: Lets a reader see how each figure was produced and why one is missing.
sections.watch_out: The schedule formula needs both dates to be present, and the approximate marker appears only when the delay was flagged as approximate.

sections.name: emitChartMetrics
sections.title: Chart coverage log
sections.what: Works out, for each project, the schedule overrun as a share of the planned duration and logs it or the reason it is missing. It also writes one summary entry saying how many projects the delivery chart can plot and why the others are missing.
sections.why: Chart readers need to know why some points are absent.
sections.watch_out: A project is only counted as plotted when both its cost deviation and its overrun percentage exist, so a missing planned duration removes it from the chart.

sections.name: FetchedField
sections.title: Shape of a stored value
sections.what: Describes one stored field: its value, its source, and for budgets the currency conversion record when the value was converted.
sections.why: Carries the value and its proof together into the fetch result.
sections.watch_out: The source can be empty, which means the value has no evidence, and later checks depend on that.

sections.name: FetchProjectEntry
sections.title: Shape of one project's fetch result
sections.what: Holds one project's identifier, name, industry, delay flags, stored fields, the Yard variance data, scan data, and the cited disclosures and forecasts that may fill gaps.
sections.why: Carries everything later stages need so they do not reread the database.
sections.watch_out: Several of these parts are optional, so code must check before using them.

sections.name: ReverifyFieldCheck
sections.title: Result of checking one value
sections.what: Holds the check outcome and the time the check ran.
sections.why: Gives reports a time stamp for each check.
sections.watch_out: The time can be empty if the value was never checked.

sections.name: ReverifyProjectEntry
sections.title: Re-check results for a project
sections.what: Holds the check result for each field of one project, and a result for each cited disclosure keyed by its evidence identifier, with an optional reason.
sections.why: Lets the workbook show whether each cited disclosure still matches its web page.
sections.watch_out: Disclosure results are keyed by evidence identifier, so a missing identifier means there is no check result for it.

sections.name: CalculateProjectEntry
sections.title: Calculated results for a project
sections.what: Holds the derived values for one project and any overrun-reason signals found in reviewed passages.
sections.why: Passes calculation output on to the finalize stage.
sections.watch_out: The reasons list is optional, and the file does not distinguish between no reasons being found and the step not running.

sections.name: PageFetchOutcome
sections.title: Result of fetching one web page
sections.what: Records whether the page was retrieved, its text, when it was checked, and the error if it failed.
sections.why: Lets later checks treat a failed page as unreachable rather than as a quote that is missing.
sections.watch_out: A failed fetch gives empty text, so checks must use the success flag rather than the text.

sections.name: fetchUniqueUrls
sections.title: Fetch many web pages with a limit
sections.what: Downloads each unique web page, with at most four running at a time, and records success or the error for each. Failed pages are added to the stage log.
sections.why: The comment describes bounded concurrency, which limits load on other sites while still moving quickly.
sections.watch_out: Failures are stored rather than thrown, so a run can finish with many unreachable pages and still report success, so the counts must be checked.

sections.name: naRecord
sections.title: Placeholder for a value that cannot be computed
sections.what: Builds a calculated record with no value, the display text N/A, and the reason and inputs used.
sections.why: Keeps every derived field present in the results, while showing honestly that it is empty.
sections.watch_out: The record is marked calculated with no value, so totals must count it as not available rather than as zero.

sections.name: inputProblem
sections.title: Why a calculation input fails
sections.what: Returns a short reason when a stored input is missing or has no evidence, and nothing when the input can be used.
sections.why: A calculation may use only sourced inputs, and this gives the reason to show when it cannot.
sections.watch_out: Presence is checked only for empty or missing values, so a zero passes as present.

sections.name: executeStage (part 1)
sections.title: Resolve scope stage
sections.what: Resolves the scope to its projects, refuses any selection that includes new projects, refuses industries that are not live, saves the run's mode, and saves the project identifiers and counts.
sections.why: The comments say new-project discovery is outside this workflow, and unsupported scopes are rejected rather than quietly filtered.
sections.watch_out: A selection with any new projects fails the whole run, so the user has to change the selection.

sections.name: executeStage (part 2)
sections.title: Start of the fetch stage
sections.what: Reads the project identifiers saved by the resolve stage, then loads each project and its active evidence quotes from the database.
sections.why: Fetching only from saved data means a resumed run gets the same input as the first attempt.
sections.watch_out: A truncation flag is fixed at false and never changes, so the output always says nothing was cut off.

sections.name: executeStage (part 3)
sections.title: Collect each project's stored values and evidence
sections.what: For each project, reads every enrichment field and keeps the value if it is present, attaching the best supporting quote. Budget fields can also be backed by budget-text quotes that pass a meaning check. It also collects reported and forecast disclosures and the held fields.
sections.why: Only values with evidence can be trusted, so unsourced values are counted openly rather than dropped.
sections.watch_out: A value with no matching quote is kept and marked as unsourced, so later checks must treat it that way.

sections.name: executeStage (part 4)
sections.title: Choose whether to research on the web
sections.what: Decides whether web research is used. It is skipped when Yard-only is chosen, or when no search provider works and no links were supplied. When skipped, the Yard data is saved as the fetch output with a clear note. Otherwise it reports the held fields and starts a research collection with saved checkpoints.
sections.why: Research is optional, so the scan should finish on Yard data and say so plainly.
sections.watch_out: The research path reuses checkpoint and cache data from the last saved summary, so an earlier failed attempt can affect what is reused.

sections.name: executeStage (part 5)
sections.title: Finish research and start re-check
sections.what: Ends the research step. It stops the run if any project's research failed, then sends the collected facts to an independent reviewer. Only facts that pass that review may feed calculations, and the summary records whether the review finished. It then begins the re-check step by reading the fetch results.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps unreviewed research out of the numbers. The code comment says that if the reviewer is unavailable, every candidate stays held out and the run says so.
sections.watch_out: If the review fails for a reason other than cancellation, all research candidates are held out, so later results may show fewer values without an error.

sections.name: executeStage (part 6)
sections.title: Collect every source page
sections.what: Gathers every unique source web address cited anywhere in the run, opens a live-feed card for each scan input and each cited Yard disclosure, and then fetches each page once. The cards let the user watch the checks happen.
sections.why: Likely reason: fetching each address once saves time and avoids repeated requests. Opening cards first lets screenshots stream in while checks run.
sections.watch_out: The cap variable is always false and the fetch list is the full list, so no limit is actually applied here.

sections.name: executeStage (part 7)
sections.title: Check each value against its page
sections.what: For each stored value that has a source, it reads the saved page text and asks three questions: is the exact quoted passage on the page, does that passage name this project, and does it state the value. A value is marked verified only if all three pass. Values with no source or no reachable page are marked that way and are not treated as evidence.
sections.why: Reason stated in the code: a value must match the live page, and a page that could not be fetched is explicitly not treated as proof.
sections.watch_out: Project matching depends on names across all scoped projects, so similar or shared names could cause a wrong pass or a wrong fail.

sections.name: executeStage (part 8)
sections.title: Record checks and decisions for values
sections.what: Stores each value's check result and writes the individual test results and an accept or not-used note to the live feed. It then runs the same kind of check on each cited Yard disclosure, including whether the passage states the needed role such as approved budget or completion. It finishes by saving each project's results and a one-line summary to the log.
sections.why: Likely reason: disclosures can also fill empty inputs, so they get the same scrutiny. The feed notes show the user why each decision was made.
sections.watch_out: Disclosure outcomes are not added to the top-level counts, so those totals understate how many checks were made.

sections.name: executeStage (part 9)
sections.title: Return re-check totals and start calculations
sections.what: Returns the re-check totals: verified, unconfirmed, unreachable and unsourced. It then starts the calculate step by loading the fetch and re-check results, building lookup tables, and noting that cost and schedule are about to be computed. It also defines a helper that treats two inputs quoting the same text as one source.
sections.why: Reason stated in the code: stored data may be partial after ingest, so every read is done field by field.
sections.watch_out: The calculate step needs saved summaries from the fetch and re-check steps, and a missing summary stops it.

sections.name: executeStage (part 10)
sections.title: Choose inputs for each project
sections.what: For each project, decides which numbers may feed cost and schedule. A Yard value is used only if it passed its check. Otherwise a live-checked cited disclosure or a reviewed research value can fill the gap, and the note records where it came from. It also decides whether the project has a final outcome and collects reviewed reasons for overruns.
sections.why: Likely reason: stronger sources are tried first (Yard, then cited disclosure, then research), and each number is labelled with its origin. The code comment says the lifecycle stage decides before the free-text status.
sections.watch_out: The final-outcome check uses word patterns, so a new status wording that is not on the list is treated as not final.

sections.name: executeStage (part 11)
sections.title: Decide the cost result
sections.what: Decides whether a project gets a cost deviation figure. If the project has a final outcome, a directly reported or research-reported overrun is preferred, and otherwise the figure is calculated from planned and actual budgets. Projects still in delivery get a labelled forecast instead. Projects that are neither final nor in delivery get not-available results for cost and schedule, each with a reason.
sections.why: Likely reason: one quoted passage cannot prove both the planned and the actual cost (the source-independence rule), and forecasts are labelled so they are not read as final results.
sections.watch_out: Cancelled, suspended or pre-investment projects show blanks rather than numbers, which a reader may take as missing data.

sections.name: executeStage (part 12)
sections.title: Convert currencies before comparing costs
sections.what: Turns each budget into millions of US dollars. When both budgets use the same non-dollar currency, the percentage is computed in that currency so exchange rate moves do not count as overrun. Otherwise each side is converted using a rate year chosen from its stated price year, an as-of year, its source date, or its milestone date, and each step is noted.
sections.why: Likely reason: budgets in different currencies or years are not comparable without conversion. The code comment states the order used to pick the rate year.
sections.watch_out: A value that shows only a dollar sign is read as US dollars by project policy, which may be wrong for some sources.

sections.name: executeStage (part 13)
sections.title: Finish cost result and start schedule
sections.what: Builds the cost result with its inputs and notes, or the reason it could not be computed. It then starts the schedule figure. It prefers a delay that was directly reported and passed its check, then a reviewed research delay, and only then calculates the delay from planned and updated completion dates.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code for this order. The effect is that stated figures are used ahead of calculated ones.
sections.watch_out: A delay flagged as approximate shows a tilde in its display, so anyone quoting it must check that flag.

sections.name: executeStage (part 14)
sections.title: Schedule months and finalize setup
sections.what: Works out the months between the planned completion date and the realised or forecast completion date. If the dates cannot be read, or name different milestones, it records a not-available reason instead. The section ends by starting the finalize step, which loads the fetch, re-check and calculate summaries.
sections.why: Likely reason: the milestone check stops a design date from being compared with a different milestone's date.
sections.watch_out: Unreadable dates become not available rather than zero, so a missing date does not look like an on-time project.

sections.name: executeStage (part 15)
sections.title: Merge checks into stored values
sections.what: The finalize step combines each re-check result with its stored Yard value to make one record per field. A value that failed its check is counted as a conflict and marked with a finding, but it is not changed. Calculated results are added to the same field list and counted in the totals.
sections.why: Reason stated in the code: an unconfirmed value is a finding, never a write, so stored data is left alone.
sections.watch_out: A field with no re-check result is treated as unsourced, so a skipped field shows as unsourced rather than causing an error.

sections.name: executeStage (part 16)
sections.title: Validate result, then synthesis and deck
sections.what: Checks the whole finalized result against a schema, and stops with an error if the shape is wrong. It then prepares the chart data. The synthesis step asks the AI model for one summary of the frozen project inputs and fails if that service is unavailable. The deck step builds editable slides from the dairy-project template.
sections.why: Reason stated in the code: saved data is never free-form, so a broken shape fails loudly before it is stored.
sections.watch_out: The synthesis step fails outright if the AI service is down, so the run cannot finish without it.

summary: Background worker that runs a Reality Scan through its ordered stages, saving progress and results to the database as it goes.
purpose: Runs a scan over a set of existing projects: checks the scope, gathers stored data and evidence, re-checks sources on the web, calculates derived figures, assembles the result, and records the run in the Yard.
why: Likely reason: each stage saves its output so that a run can survive a restart and be resumed, and a database lock stops the same run from running twice. The header comments describe this design.
how: The run goes through the stage list in order. It first resolves the scope to its projects, then fetches stored values and evidence from the Yard, then re-checks sourced values against their web pages, then calculates cost deviation and schedule overrun from sourced inputs, then finalizes the result and chart figures, then synthesizes and builds the deck model. At the end it records the run in the Yard and marks it succeeded. The start function takes a lock and launches the stages in the background.
inputs: A run identifier and its saved scope; projects, evidence quotes and Yard data read from the database; web pages fetched through the safe fetch helper; search providers; and any links the user supplied as primary sources.
outputs: Stage rows with status, output, log lines and usage; events for the live feed; the run status (queued, running, succeeded, failed or cancelled); a record of the run in the Yard; and console log lines.
risks: The fetch stage sets a truncation flag to false and never changes it. The header says the scan is read-only, yet the last step records the run in the Yard, and this file does not show what that writes, so that is unclear. A stage failure stops the run and leaves later stages unrun until someone starts it again.
debug: Search the server log for lines containing crashed, stage failed or Yard record failed. Open the stage row for the failed stage, since its log holds the error message. If a run stays in running, check whether the lock for that run is still held. A message about a prerequisite stage having no saved summary means stages ran out of order or were damaged, so starting the run again may help. Research being skipped appears as a note in the fetch stage summary.
